analysis.one_liner: Expands children's online privacy law to cover all teens under 18, requires parental or teen consent for data collection, and bans targeted ads to minors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have updated the 1998 children's online privacy law, which currently only protects kids under 13. It would have extended protections to everyone under 18: websites and apps would need clear, specific permission from a teen or a parent before collecting a young person's data; they could no longer use that data to target ads at minors; and teens and parents could demand to see, correct, or delete the data held about them. The bill also would have raised fines to $63,795 per violation, let the FTC create a dedicated youth privacy office, and given parents the right to sue companies that broke the rules. It never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers under 18, and their parents, would gain meaningful control over the data that websites, apps, and online services collect about them: no targeted ads built on their behavior, the right to see and delete what companies hold, and the power to sue if companies violate the rules. The Federal Trade Commission would also gain a dedicated office and higher penalties to enforce these rights.

how_it_helps.text: It requires digital services to get express, specific, informed consent — from a teenager directly, or from a parent for a child under 13 — before processing the young person's personal information, and lets teens or parents withdraw that consent.

It bans targeted personalized advertising to children and teenagers based on their data, online behavior, or characteristics they share with other young people, including income level or protected traits.
It gives teenagers and parents the right to see what data a service holds about them, find out which third parties received it, and have it corrected or deleted within 45 days of a request.

It raises the maximum civil penalty per violation to $63,795, gives the FTC a dedicated Youth Privacy and Marketing Division, and creates a private right of action so families can sue violators and recover damages and attorney's fees.

It requires services aimed at or likely used by kids to minimize the data they collect, adopt reasonable security practices, limit data retention, and assess and mitigate risks to young users before and after launch.

analysis.who_pays: Internet platforms, app makers, advertising technology firms, and data brokers would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to target personalized ads at minors, would have to redesign their data practices, run privacy impact assessments, and could face lawsuits and fines up to $63,795 per violation.

drawbacks.text: Requiring 'age assurance' to determine which users are under 18 would force services to verify or estimate users' ages, which means collecting and processing additional identity data — a privacy cost that falls on all users of a service, not just children.

The private right of action allows parents to sue for any violation, with actual and punitive damages, injunctions, and attorney's fees, and invalidates pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers — a broad litigation exposure that critics said could invite lawsuits over technical violations rather than real harms.

The compliance burden — privacy impact assessments, plain-language policies, data minimization, security programs, and annual reviews — would fall on every covered organization, including nonprofits and small operators, not only the largest platforms.

Extending restrictions on 'targeted personalized advertising' and other marketing to everyone under 18 raised free-speech and overbreadth concerns, since the bill treats 17-year-olds the same as small children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for families are real: under current law the main children's online privacy statute only covers kids under 13, so teenagers' data is essentially unprotected, and this bill would have extended consent, access, deletion, and anti-tracking protections to everyone under 18 [S2][S3]. The costs are serious and honest supporters should acknowledge them. Age assurance for teens sits in tension with anonymity: to keep teens' data safe, services may have to verify more identities, which itself creates new privacy risks for everyone [S3]. The private right of action, with punitive damages and no forced arbitration, could produce a wave of lawsuits against companies for technical violations rather than improved practices [S3]. And the compliance burden falls on small websites and app makers as much as on the big platforms the bill targets. On balance the bill would likely have shifted real power over minors' data from platforms and advertisers back to families, at the cost of some new friction, litigation risk, and more identity checks online.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On July 30, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce; the action history records no hearing, markup, or floor vote afterward.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill advancing further, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet platforms, ad-tech firms, and data brokers are better off: none of the consent, anti-targeting, or deletion requirements ever took effect, and their ability to collect and monetize data on users under 18 remained largely unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet platforms and the ad-tech industry

for.name: Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the core provisions extending children's privacy protections to teens and banning targeted ads to minors.

for.name: 27 of 435 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, so it never advanced out of committee.

against.name: Internet platforms and the ad-tech industry
against.role: Social media, advertising, and data-broker companies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against broad new children's privacy mandates and a private right of action during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists — its fate was decided in committee, where the Democratic chair did not advance it.

industries.note: The bill bans targeted personalized advertising to anyone under 18 and bars using kids' data, behavior, or shared characteristics (including income) for marketing — cutting off a core revenue stream built on profiling young users [S2][S3]. If it had passed, ads shown to minors would have had to rely on context rather than surveillance.

Platforms would face consent requirements for all users under 18 (up from under 13 today), data minimization, deletion and correction rights, 'best interests of the child' design duties, risk assessments, and potential lawsuits by parents — a substantial redesign of how their services treat minors [S2][S3].

Services would have to disclose whether they send children's and teens' data to data brokers, and the bill's written-agreement and disclosure requirements would restrict the sale and onward transfer of young people's information [S3].

The bill's age-assurance, impact-assessment, and audit requirements would have created demand for verification tools and compliance consulting — though the FTC must approve age-assurance methods and require that age data be minimized and destroyed [S3].
